The memorandum should separate termination, maternity, working-time, holiday and wage claims. Section 3 of the Shop and Office Employees Act ordinarily limits normal work to eight hours per day and forty-five hours per week, excluding rest or meal intervals, subject to applicable regulations. Section 5 provides a whole weekly holiday and a half-holiday, with full remuneration where the employee worked at least twenty-eight non-overtime hours. Section 6 governs annual holiday and leave, including fourteen days in a second or subsequent year and up to seven days' leave for private business, ill health or another reasonable cause, subject to its conditions.

Because the claimant is a shop employee, Part IA of the Shop and Office Employees Act supplies the maternity regime. Section 18B provides pregnancy and confinement leave, including seventy days from confinement where a live child is delivered and twenty-eight days where no live child is delivered; Section 18C requires full remuneration for the statutory leave. Section 18E prohibits termination by reason only of pregnancy, confinement or consequential illness and places on the employer, in a prosecution, the burden of proving another cause. Section 18F prohibits notice of dismissal during Part IA leave or notice timed to expire during that leave. The Maternity Benefits Ordinance should not be presented as the governing maternity statute for this shop employee.

From 1 January 2026 the national minimum monthly wage is Rs. 30,000 and the daily wage is Rs. 1,200. A payment of Rs. 27,000 therefore falls below the national monthly floor, subject to accurate proof of the employment period and classification. Budgetary-relief allowances existing on 31 March 2025 are consolidated as part of the wage, and the 2025 amendment prevents wage reduction that would negate the increase.

Under Section 31B of the Industrial Disputes Act, the worker or her union may apply to a Labour Tribunal concerning termination and identified termination benefits. The application must be filed within six months of termination. The Tribunal may grant relief notwithstanding contrary contractual terms and is to make a just and equitable order after inquiry. Section 31B(5) requires careful election of remedies: after Tribunal proceedings are entertained and concluded, another remedy for the same matter is unavailable, and prior resort to another legal remedy bars the Section 31B route. The memorandum should distinguish reinstatement, compensation, wages or benefits and statutory enforcement, preserve payroll, attendance, leave and pregnancy-related communications, and avoid double recovery.

results.question: Prepare a conveyancing and litigation-risk memorandum for a purchaser proposing to acquire an undivided interest in land originally alienated by the State on a permit. The permit-holder has signed a private sale deed, a partition action concerning the land is registered as a lis pendens, a competing deed is presented for registration, and the purchaser proposes to lodge a priority notice. Explain validity, registration priority, the effect of lis pendens, and why registration cannot cure a defective or prohibited disposition.

output.answer:
## Executive Summary

This memorandum addresses the legal risks associated with acquiring an interest in State land originally alienated under a permit. Under the Land Development Ordinance, such land is subject to strict alienation controls, and unauthorized private transfers are legally precarious. Furthermore, the presence of a registered *lis pendens* and competing deeds necessitates caution, as registration under the Registration of Documents Ordinance does not validate an otherwise void or prohibited disposition. Prospective purchasers must ensure compliance with statutory approval requirements to avoid the invalidation of their interest.

## Findings

### Legal Validity and Alienability of State Land
Under Section 19 of the Land Development Ordinance, State land is initially alienated via a permit authorizing occupation. A permit-holder is subject to specific conditions regarding the disposal of the holding. Specifically, under Section 3(6)(b) of the Land Development Ordinance, a permit-holder (or owner of a holding under a grant) is prohibited from disposing of such holding without the prior approval of the Government Agent. While exceptions exist for mortgaging to specific licensed commercial banks or prescribed institutions under Section 3(7) of the Land Development Ordinance, a private sale deed executed without the requisite Government Agent's approval may be considered a prohibited disposition. Additionally, under Section 161 of the Land Development Ordinance, no prescriptive title can be acquired against the State or any other person regarding land alienated on a permit.

### Effect of Lis Pendens and Competing Deeds
Under Section 11(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, a *lis pendens* (a pending action) relating to land does not bind a purchaser unless it is duly registered. Once registered, the action is deemed pending from the time of registration, regardless of whether the summons has been served [LAW-6]. Regarding competing deeds, Section 7(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance provides that an instrument is void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration by virtue of a subsequent instrument that is duly registered. However, this priority is subject to the caveat that fraud or collusion in securing prior registration will defeat such priority [LAW-14].

### Efficacy of Priority Notices and Registration Limits
Under Section 30(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, a purchaser may lodge a 'priority notice' to protect an interest before the execution of an instrument. If an instrument is subsequently registered while the priority notice is in force, it is deemed to have been registered at the time the priority notice was registered [LAW-11]. Crucially, however, Section 7(4) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance explicitly states that the registration of an instrument does not cure any defect in the instrument or confer upon it any effect or validity which it would not otherwise have. Consequently, if the underlying disposition is prohibited under the Land Development Ordinance (e.g., lack of Government Agent approval), registration—even with a priority notice—cannot validate the transaction.

## Conclusion

The proposed acquisition is high-risk. The purchaser must verify if the permit-holder has obtained the necessary approval from the Government Agent as required by Section 3(6)(b) of the Land Development Ordinance. The existence of a registered *lis pendens* indicates ongoing litigation that may affect the title, and the purchaser should be aware that registration under the Registration of Documents Ordinance provides priority but does not cure the fundamental illegality of a prohibited disposition under Section 7(4) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance.

results.ground_truth:
The memorandum should begin with the source of title. Under Section 46(1) of the Land Development Ordinance, a permit-holder may not dispose of permit land. The limited exception in Section 46(2) permits, with the Government Agent's written consent, a mortgage to a registered society of which the permit-holder is a member. Any other disposition is null and void under Section 46(3). A private sale to the proposed purchaser therefore cannot be validated merely by notarial form or registration.

A valid transaction affecting ordinary immovable property generally must satisfy Section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance. Rohan de Soyza v. Jinendradasa illustrates that execution before an unlicensed notary and failure of the executant, witnesses and notary to sign in one another's presence render the deed defective. Section 7(4) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance confirms that registration does not cure a defect or confer validity beyond the statutory priority effect.

Priority and validity must be distinguished. Under Section 7(1), an unregistered instrument is void against a subsequent adverse instrument acquired for value and duly registered, but fraud or collusion defeats the later instrument's priority under Section 7(2). Section 30 allows a transferee to register a priority notice before execution with the transferor's written consent, or after execution without it. A qualifying instrument registered while the notice is in force is treated as registered at the time of the notice. The notice lasts six weeks, may be renewed for another six weeks, and lapses if no instrument is registered while it remains in force. None of those priority effects can transform a Land Development Ordinance disposition that is substantively null.

Section 66 of the Partition Law creates a separate prohibition after registration of the partition action as a lis pendens. A voluntary alienation, lease or hypothecation of an undivided share is prohibited pending final determination and is void, although it is deemed valid if the partition action is dismissed. The purchaser should not complete. The correct roadmap is to verify the State grant or permit and its conditions, obtain the Land Registry and partition records, determine whether any statutory disposition route exists, and seek case-specific court or administrative relief rather than relying on registration priority.

results.question: Prepare a comparative commercial-law memorandum explaining how the attached Sri Lankan authorities treat five different stages of a transaction: whether an incorporeal trading right is 'goods'; when conditional non-payment amounts to repudiation of an instalment contract; what a seller must prove before recovering for non-acceptance; when actions on a mortgage and a written guarantee prescribe; and when a statutory bank-sale certificate passes title without a notarial conveyance.

output.answer:
## Executive Summary
This memorandum addresses key commercial law principles under Sri Lankan statutes. Findings indicate that while the Sale of Goods Ordinance No. 11 of 1896 governs the sale of goods, it does not explicitly define 'incorporeal rights' as goods. Statutory bank-sale certificates are recognized as valid instruments for title transfer, overriding the general requirement for notarial conveyance under the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance [LAW-6, LAW-7, LAW-10]. Prescription periods are strictly defined, with ten years for mortgages and six years for written contracts [LAW-11, LAW-12, LAW-13].

## Findings

### 1. Definition of 'Goods' and Incorporeal Rights
The Sale of Goods Ordinance No. 11 of 1896 provides for the sale of 'goods', which includes 'existing goods' or 'future goods' to be manufactured or acquired [LAW-3]. The provided source documents do not explicitly define whether 'incorporeal rights' fall within the definition of 'goods'. Consequently, the provided authorities are insufficient to determine the status of incorporeal rights under the Sale of Goods Ordinance No. 11 of 1896.

### 2. Repudiatory Breach in Instalment Contracts
The provided source documents do not contain specific criteria regarding what constitutes a 'repudiatory breach' in the context of instalment contracts. While the Sale of Goods Ordinance No. 11 of 1896 outlines rights of an unpaid seller, it does not detail the threshold for repudiation in instalment-based agreements.

### 3. Recovery for Non-Acceptance
Under Section 47(3) of the Sale of Goods Ordinance No. 11 of 1896, an unpaid seller may resell goods and recover damages for non-acceptance if the goods are of a perishable nature, or if the seller has given notice of the intention to resell and the buyer fails to pay or tender the price within a reasonable time [LAW-4].

### 4. Prescription Periods
- **Mortgages:** Under Section 5 of the Prescription Ordinance No. 22 of 1871, actions upon any hypothecation or mortgage must be commenced within ten years from the date of the instrument or the breach of condition [LAW-11, LAW-13].
- **Written Guarantees/Contracts:** Under Section 6 of the Prescription Ordinance No. 22 of 1871, actions upon a written promise, contract, or other written security (not falling under Section 5) must be brought within six years from the date of the breach [LAW-12].

### 5. Statutory Bank-Sale Certificates
Under Section 55 of the National Savings Bank Act No. 30 of 1971, a certificate of sale signed by the Bank is legally valid and passes title to immovable property by operation of law, notwithstanding the general requirement for a notarial conveyance under the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance [LAW-6, LAW-7, LAW-10]. Similarly, the Recovery of Loans by Banks (Special Provisions) Act No. 4 of 1990 provides for the issuance of certificates of sale that facilitate the transfer of title [LAW-9].

## Conclusion
The legal framework in Sri Lanka provides specific statutory mechanisms for bank-led property recovery that bypass traditional notarial requirements [LAW-6, LAW-10]. Commercial transactions involving the sale of goods are governed by the Sale of Goods Ordinance No. 11 of 1896, which mandates specific conditions for resale and damages [LAW-4]. Prescription periods are strictly enforced, with a ten-year limit for mortgage-related actions and a six-year limit for general written contracts [LAW-12, LAW-13].

results.ground_truth:
Croos v. De Soysa treats the right to sell arrack within a district for a defined period as an incorporeal right rather than 'goods' under the Sale of Goods Ordinance. The Ordinance's concept of goods concerns tangible or corporeal movables. The verbal agreement for the trading right was therefore not unenforceable under the Sale of Goods writing rule applicable to goods.

Fernando v. Mendis distinguishes a mere delayed payment from conduct showing repudiation. The purchaser refused to pay for deliveries unless the seller supplied an indemnity or guarantee not required by the contract. That qualified refusal demonstrated an intention not to be bound and justified withholding later deliveries. The controlling inquiry is the intention revealed by the circumstances, not non-payment in isolation.

Rawanna & Co. v. Arunachapillai applies Section 37 of the Sale of Goods Ordinance. A seller claiming loss for a buyer's non-acceptance must prove both readiness and willingness to deliver and a request to the buyer to take delivery. Goods not actually available at the agreed store and the absence of a request defeated the seller's counterclaim.

Hatton National Bank Ltd. v. Sellers Sports distinguishes the secured obligations for prescription. An action enforcing the mortgage fell under Section 5 of the Prescription Ordinance and carried the ten-year period. The written guarantee fell under Section 6 and carried six years. Because the guarantee made payment due ten days after written demand, prescription on the guarantee ran from the breach following that demand, not from the principal debtor's earlier default.

Abeykoon v. National Savings Bank holds that a certificate of sale under Section 55 of the National Savings Bank Act passes title by operation of law. The special statutory disposition does not require the ordinary notarial conveyance contemplated by Section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance. The memo should keep these doctrines distinct: classification and form, repudiation, tender and demand, computation of prescription, and statutory transfer of title answer different stages and should not be collapsed into one general contract rule.
